newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY ENERGY INVESTORS SET TO CHALLENGE HIKES.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY ENERGY INVESTORS SET TO CHALLENGE HIKES.

text.p: Western investors in Hungary's utilities are to appeal to the government over January wholesale energy price rises which they say do not allow them the profit margins guaranteed when they bought into the sector.

"We have certainly not had the last word on the subject," Tibor Tamas, president of the Gas Producers Association, told Reuters. "We and our Western investors believe this will not give us the margins we had been promised."

The government announced in November retail hikes for distributors of 24.9 percent for electricity and 18.8 percent for gas but did not define the margins which would be granted to energy producers and distributors until December 21.
The new margins translate into increases in the price distributors have to pay for the energy they sell to consumers of around 18.3 percent for electricity and 16.9 percent for gas.

Companies such as Electricite de France (EdF), Gaz de France and German electricity giant RWE invested a total of more than $2 billion in Hungary's energy distribution network a year ago and were promised an eight percent return on investment from January 1997.

The chairman of the exclusive supplier of gas to the distributors, oil and gas company MOL Rt , described the wholesale price rises as "correct" but the Western investors said they planned to initiate talks with the government because the wholesale hikes were too high.
Tamas said the distribution companies had been invited by the Industry and Trade Ministry to open talks with the Hungarian Energy Office if they felt the margins were insufficient.
"Members of the gas producers will meet this week to come to a common position," he said, adding that the wholesale price increase was high relative to the retail hike.
"The difference between 16.9 percent and 18.8 percent is very small," he said.

Pierre Abou, representative in Hungary of EdF, which has just under 50 percent stakes in two regional electricity distribution companies, said the Western investors were looking for a separate meeting directly with the government "at the highest possible level" and would meet jointly.
"We will resume talks with the government in early January and negotiate together," Abou told Reuters, adding that EdF's future investments in Hungary will depend on the outcome of the talks.
Abou said the main bone of contention was how costs were incorporated into the formula used to calculate the prices.
"We are satisfied with the formula, it's the implementation, particularly cost assessment, that's the problem," he said, adding that inflation forecasts and wage costs were underestimated.
"We want real costs included -- not would-be inflation but real inflation, not would-be costs but real costs," he said.

Andreas Przetak, manager of the Budapest office of RWE, which also has large stakes in two distributing companies, told Reuters that his company was pushing for the inclusion of interest payments on loans taken out on the investment as well as insurance payments for running the network.
Przetak said that while RWE was still dissatisfied with the margins, the position was not as bad as seemed likely when the government cancelled a planned energy price rise for October.
"Things are looking better than in October as the increase was a little bit higher than we expected but I must say we are still not happy," he said.

Belgian utility Tractebel , which owns 48 percent of the oil-fired Dunamenti power station, is currently involved in separate talks with the state privatisation agency APV over the price it is to receive for the power it supplies to the Hungary's electricity company MVM.
MVM sells on the electricity to the distributors.

Tractebel claims it is making huge losses on the operation as it buys its oil from MOL at market rates which it says will not be covered by the 34.5 percent increase it is to be granted for its energy from Thursday.
Last month the Belgian group said it was considering suing Hungary over the government's energy pricing policy and could pull out it continues to make losses.
Tractebel's representative in Hungary Tibor Kuhl told Reuters the company's position will be clear within two weeks.
"We will make our position public within a week or two," he said.
